text:
Surgical technique innovations are typically associated with no additional costs but are generally associated with improved quality of care. However, it remains unclear whether mini-laparoscopic surgery (MLS) for colorectal cancer (CRC) is more cost-effective than conventional open surgery in the year following resection. This study aimed to assess cost-effectiveness by comparing MLS to open surgery using a prospective, non-randomized, cohort design at an academic medical center.

A total of 551 patients (224 undergoing MLS and 339 undergoing open surgery) were included; after propensity score matching, 212 patient pairs formed the analysis cohort. Costs were measured using hospital-index charges and outpatient and inpatient expenditures over one year post-discharge. Effectiveness was evaluated via life-years gained and quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs) gained.

Incremental costs and effectiveness were estimated via difference analysis between MLS and open surgery using adjusted predictions.

Among patients who underwent MLS, transfusion rates were lower, complications were less frequent, hospital stays shorter, and overall medical costs within the first year were significantly reduced (TWD 748,269, USD 24,942 per QALY, p=0.045) compared to open surgery. These results support the conclusion that mini-laparoscopic surgery is both cost-saving and more effective in terms of quality-adjusted life years for CRC patients after resection.

text: The study examined the defensive secretions of two millipede species, Pachyiulus hungaricus and Megaphyllum unilineatum, focusing on their antioxidant and enzyme inhibitory properties. Extracts prepared from secretions using ethanol, methanol, hexane, and dichloromethane were assessed via ABTS, DPPH radical-scavenging assays, and total reducing power (TRP) tests. Additionally, acetylcholinesterase and tyrosinase inhibition activities were measured, and antifungal effects against seven Fusarium species were evaluated. Results demonstrated that both species’ secretions exhibited free radical-scavenging activity and inhibited acetylcholinesterase and tyrosinase, though differences in antioxidant potency were observed: P. hungaricus showed stronger antioxidative effects than M. unilineatum. Inhibition of tyrosinase was more pronounced in the hexane extract of M. unilineatum compared to P. hungaricus. Among tested Fusarium strains, F. sporotrichioides, F. graminearum, and F. verticillioides were most resistant to both secretions. Notably, F. avenaceum was the most sensitive to P. hungaricus, whereas the hexane extract of M. unilineatum required the lowest concentrations to inhibit F. lateritium. These findings confirm the antimicrobial and neuroprotective capacities of julid defensive secretions and suggest additional bioactivities may be present due to their complex chemical composition.

Fusarium sporotrichioides, F. graminearum, and F. verticillioides were the fungi most resistant to secretions of both julids. The Fusarium species most susceptible to the secretion of P. hungaricus was F. avenaceum, while the concentrations of M. unilienatum extracts needed to inhibit and completely suppress fungal growth were lowest in the case of their action on F. lateritium. Our data support previous findings that julid defensive secretions possess an antimicrobial potential and reveal their antioxidative and antineurodegenrative properties. France’s elections have historically followed a simple ritual: voters enter a booth, mark their ballot by hand on a pre-printed slip, fold it into an envelope, and hand it to an official. After verifying identity, the official places the envelope into a transparent ballot box. A signature is then recorded in a logbook to confirm the voter’s presence. The process, unchanged for decades, relies on physical visibility and human oversight.

Since 1988, law has required that ballot boxes remain visibly empty at the start of voting. Officials and observers must be able to see that no ballots are inside before the first envelope is dropped. During the count, only sealed envelopes may be added, and every step is open to inspection by representatives from each candidate’s campaign. After the polls close, counts are conducted in the evening by volunteers—elected or appointed—under close supervision to prevent error or manipulation.

This year, that system faces challenge. The presidential vote now includes electronic voting machines, a shift that has sparked fierce debate. Critics—many of them computer scientists and civil society advocates—note that machines remove the direct traceability of individual votes. Paper ballots, once seen and handled by many, are now processed behind digital screens. The absence of a physical paper trail makes it difficult to verify that each vote was counted exactly as cast. These concerns are not new, but they’ve sharpened as machines play a larger role.

The legal framework for approving these machines is itself under scrutiny. Approval rests on internal technical reports submitted by private vendors—reports not subject to public review. The Ministry of the Interior, which signs off on these devices, is currently led by Nicolas Sarkozy, one of the leading presidential candidates. His role in overseeing the very technology used in the election has raised questions about impartiality.

All major opposition parties have rejected the machines, while the ruling UMP party has not. Some voters have filed lawsuits to block deployment, citing technical flaws and procedural breaches. A group of opposition activists has published a detailed field guide for observers, specifying which model numbers and software versions must be used, and outlining how to confirm compliance at polling stations. The controversy peaked on April 12, when the Ministry abruptly authorized a single model of machine, reportedly in response to pressure.

Supporters, including the group France Élection, argue that machines reduce paper waste, cut down on manual labor, and speed up results. They dismiss claims of fraud as alarmist. But the final word may rest with the Constitutional Council, which must decide whether any votes cast on machines not officially approved will be invalidated. The debate isn’t just about technology—it’s about whether the public can still see how votes are counted, and whether trust in the system can survive when the process disappears behind a screen.

text: We examined strategies to reduce accumulation of misfolded α1-antitrypsin Z (ATZ), a key factor in classical α1-antitrypsin deficiency (ATD) that drives liver damage. Using a *C. elegans* model of ATD, we conducted a genome-wide RNA interference screen combined with systems pharmacology analysis to identify genetic regulators of ATZ buildup and predict repurposable drugs. The screen revealed glibenclamide (GLB), a sulfonylurea commonly used to treat type 2 diabetes, as a candidate that reduces ATZ levels. In human cell lines expressing ATZ, GLB increased autophagic degradation of the misfolded protein. An analog of GLB was tested in a mouse model of ATD and reduced hepatic ATZ deposits and fibrosis, without affecting systemic glucose or insulin concentrations. These results indicate that simple invertebrate models, when paired with genetic and computational screening, can yield actionable insights into human disease mechanisms. The data support advancing GLB and its structural analogs into clinical trials for ATD-related liver disease, where they may slow or halt progression without metabolic side effects.

text: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1A (CMT1A), the most common variant, stems from a duplication of the PMP22 gene, leading to impaired myelination, axonal degeneration, and steadily worsening muscle weakness. No treatments are currently approved for CMT1A. Earlier studies showed that PXT3003—a mix of baclofen, naltrexone, and sorbitol—slowed disease progression in adult Pmp22 transgenic rats, a well-validated model of CMT1A. Here, we tested whether initiating PXT3003 shortly after birth could alter disease onset. Rats received daily oral doses from postnatal day 6 to 18, with assessments extended through 12 weeks. A brief two-week intervention led to a striking recovery in motor performance, with treated animals matching wildtype levels. Histology confirmed a normalization of axon calibre, particularly in motor axons, which shifted from a broad, irregular distribution toward a more robust, uniform size. Distal motor latencies improved electrophysiologically, aligning with behavioral gains. At the molecular level, PXT3003 reduced the overexpression of Pmp22 mRNA and restored balance to the PI3K-AKT and MEK-ERK signalling pathways. This correction may have supported Schwann cell maturation, potentially preserving axonal integrity. These results indicate that a short course of PXT3003 in early life can substantially reduce both clinical and molecular signs of CMT1A. With a favorable safety record and ongoing phase III trials in human patients, PXT3003 emerges as a viable option for younger individuals with CMT1A.

This study examined how well different measures of body fat predict metabolic syndrome (MetS) in people already at moderate cardiovascular risk, a group where obesity is known to raise the chance of death and heart problems. Data came from 2,478 individuals in the MARK study, where body fat was assessed using five methods: body mass index (BMI), waist-to-height ratio (WHtR), CUN-BAE, body roundness index (BRI), and body shape index (ABSI). MetS was diagnosed using the NCEP-ATP III criteria.

The strength of the link between these measures and blood sugar markers—HbA1c and fasting plasma glucose—varied, with correlation coefficients between 0.155 and 0.320. ABSI showed weaker associations across the board, especially in men. Diagnostic accuracy, measured by the area under the ROC curve, ranged from 0.773 (BMI in men) to 0.567 (ABSI in men). After adjusting for factors like age, sex, and lifestyle, all adiposity indicators except ABSI predicted MetS with similar strength. CUN-BAE had the highest overall odds ratio (OR) for MetS (5.50; 95% CI 4.27–7.09). In men, BMI had the strongest association (OR 5.98; 95% CI 4.70–7.60), while in women, WHtR and BRI were most predictive (OR 4.15; 95% CI 3.09–5.58). These results indicate that most adiposity measures perform similarly in detecting MetS in this population, but ABSI does not.

text:
Late embryogenesis abundant (LEA) proteins function as molecular shields, shielding cellular components during dehydration and other abiotic stresses. In Sorghum bicolor, a systematic survey detected 68 LEA-encoding genes, grouped into eight distinct families. The LEA-2 family, characterized by hydrophobic domains, dominates the repertoire. These genes are scattered across all ten chromosomes, with clusters concentrated on chromosomes 1, 2, and 3. Nearly all SbLEA genes lack introns or contain only one or two, suggesting a history of retrotransposition or minimal splicing complexity.

Gene duplication events, primarily segmental, account for 22 major genomic segments, with the SbLEA-2 family showing the most pronounced expansion. Orthology comparisons identified 12 genes shared with Arabidopsis thaliana and 13 with Oryza sativa, indicating deep conservation across grasses. Most SbLEA proteins are basic and localized to the chloroplast, implicating roles in photosynthetic tissue protection.

A network of 15 microRNAs targets 25 of the SbLEA genes, linking them to developmental regulation and stress adaptation. Promoter regions contain diverse cis-elements: DRE, MYB, MYC, and GT1 for abiotic stress; W-Box for pathogen responses; ABA-, ERE-, and TGA-responsive elements for hormone signaling; and SKn for developmental cues. This suggests LEA genes integrate inputs from multiple stress and growth pathways.

Expression profiling from microarray data across roots, pith, rind, internode, shoot, and leaf reveals sharp differences in gene activity depending on tissue type. qRT-PCR confirmed strong expression in roots, stems, and leaves, with stems showing the highest transcript levels. Under drought, salt, and cold stress, most SbLEA genes increase in expression—often in multiple tissues. SbLEA3-2 stands out with sustained high expression across diverse stress conditions. The findings clarify how SbLEA genes evolved and how they contribute to stress resilience and development in sorghum, setting a foundation for further functional dissection.

For marine conservation to use these records effectively, future initiatives must retain the same rigor in both collection and interpretation.

text: Vaccine efficacy (VE) estimates are essential for deciding whether dengue vaccines should be deployed in public health programs. But standard trial analyses can misrepresent true efficacy when they ignore how unevenly people encounter dengue virus. We built an agent-based transmission model using long-term entomological and epidemiological data from Iquitos, Peru, to simulate city-wide dengue vaccine trials with a known true VE of 0.8. In 1,000 independently generated trials—each designed for 90% power—we found that conventional methods underestimated VE by as much as 21% when exposure variation across individuals wasn’t factored in. When we included individual exposure counts from both vaccine and placebo groups, the bias disappeared. Modeling exposure heterogeneity with a frailty random effect reduced the bias but didn’t eliminate it entirely. A separate issue emerged from differences in how infections were detected: vaccinated seronegative individuals had fewer detectable primary infections, likely because their immune systems cleared viremia faster than in seropositive individuals experiencing secondary infections. This made VE appear higher in the seronegative group—about 1% above the seropositive group. These results show that trial interpretations must directly address both exposure variability and differences in infection detectability to avoid misleading conclusions.

The lexical tones remained unchanged across conditions, isolating pitch contour as the variable. Participants identified final keywords in sentences masked by either two-talker babble or steady-state noise. Recognition was consistently highest when the original fundamental frequency (F0) contour was used, outperforming both reduced and amplified pitch patterns. The degradation in performance was more severe under two-talker babble when pitch contours were exaggerated, suggesting that unnatural pitch movements interfere with the brain’s ability to separate voices in complex auditory settings. Even with correct lexical tones, distorted intonation reduces the capacity to extract speech from competing voices. These results indicate that natural prosody is not merely stylistic—it is essential for speech perception in real-world listening environments, especially when multiple voices overlap.

text:
Ronnie Miller hadn’t spoken to her father in three years. The divorce had cracked their family wide open, and her mother, tired of the silence, made the decision that summer: Ronnie and her younger brother, Jonah, would go live with Steve in Wrightsville, North Carolina. Ronnie didn’t want to go. She’d built a life in New York, and her father had become a distant figure—someone she’d stopped expecting anything from.

She arrived with her arms crossed and her eyes fixed on the ground. Her father tried to talk, to show her the house, to bring up old memories, but she shut him down with cold politeness. She told him she’d leave by mid-August if he didn’t stop pretending they were close.

Then she met Will. He wasn’t who she thought she’d fall for—quiet, wore glasses, worked at the library. But something in the way he looked at her, not with pity or expectation, made her stop holding her breath. They started walking after school, then talking past midnight on her bedroom floor. For the first time, she felt something like peace.

That peace cracked when Steve was diagnosed with stage three stomach cancer. The news came in a hospital hallway, just after they’d finished the stained-glass window for his church—the one he’d started while recovering from surgery. Ronnie worked on it with Jonah, her hands stained with blue and gold, her thoughts full of her father’s quiet strength.

After the summer, Jonah returned to New York with their mother. Ronnie stayed. She helped him sleep through the nights, read aloud from old journals, made tea that never got cold. When he died, she sat at the piano and played the melody he’d left behind—a fragment, a half-remembered tune.

Will came to the funeral. They didn’t speak. Afterward, he went back to Ohio. She thought that was it.

Then, in late January, she got a letter. He’d transferred to a college in Manhattan. She didn’t reply. But she started writing songs again.

After days, he finds a high fortress carved into the side of a cliff, the home of Kashchei the Immortal. Inside, he meets Princess Tatiana, known across the lands as the most beautiful woman alive. He pretends to be slow, clumsy, and easily fooled. When he brings her out, she is safe. But he feels no longing. He does not look back as he leaves.

Zachary Wallace, a marine biologist from the American Southeast, joined a research dive into the Sargasso Sea to gather footage of giant squids. The sub descended beneath a still, sunless surface. Sonar picked up a signal long tagged as the Bloop—a deep, irregular pulse recorded years before. As the sound grew louder, pressure sensors spiked. Through the acrylic dome, Wallace and the two others—Hank, a dive engineer, and the pilot—watched as a colossal squid thrashed in the dark, torn apart by creatures that left no trace on the hull. The dome cracked under unseen force. They surged upward, scrambling through the hatch. The pressure shift came too fast. The dome ruptured mid-ascent. The cabin flooded. The pilot was gone before the water reached the neck. Wallace went under, choked, then gasped awake in Hank’s grip. He lived.

Back in Fort Lauderdale, Wallace took a teaching post at Florida Atlantic University. He learned, through hushed conversations and dropped syllabi, that David, a former mentor and close confidant, believed Wallace had ignored warning signs during the dive—hadn’t overridden the autopilot. David blamed him for the sub’s loss and the pilot’s death. After a year, the university severed ties. Wallace spent the next months drinking alone in bars near the coast, moving through bars and cathedrals, spending every last dollar on motion and noise.

Then he heard: Angus Wallace, his father, was on trial in Inverness for murdering a fisherman near Loch Ness. They hadn’t spoken since his mother left Scotland seventeen years prior, returning to the U.S. alone. But the half-brother, now a student at Glasgow, had reached out—said Angus needed him at the hearing. Zachary boarded a flight.

He reconnected with old contacts in Miami—women who used to work on lab projects, men who’d seen him at conferences. He started gathering old letters, checking old contacts via email, trying to piece together what had happened to his family. Then Angus took the stand. He said he’d seen the dead man attacked by something in the loch—something with a neck long enough to arch over the water. The press caught fire. News crews swarmed the Highlands. Boats lined the loch, their wakes churning the surface.

With no academic future, and little left but memory and questions, Wallace decided to follow the threads. He’d look into the testimony, the dead man’s contacts, the Black Knights—those who still met in stone halls deep in the Scottish hills. He’d find what the others had buried. Not just to clear his father. To understand what had happened to him.

text:
The Eastern Conference bested the Western Conference in the 2008 NBA All-Star Game, played at the New Orleans Arena in Louisiana. The final score was 134-128, with the East holding on after a late surge from the West. Down by 13 points at the beginning of the fourth quarter, the West closed the gap largely through the efforts of New Orleans’ Chris Paul, who dished out seven assists in the period. With 2:48 left, Paul found Brandon Roy for a layup that gave the West a 122-119 lead—their highest point in the game.

The East answered quickly, with back-to-back three-pointers from Ray Allen. Paul responded with a three of his own, but the momentum had shifted. Dwyane Wade scored a layup, Allen sank another three, and LeBron James drove in for a dunk. With 8.7 seconds remaining, Roy hit another three, cutting the deficit to three. Allen then made all three free throws, sealing the win for the East.

The game was the main event of a weekend packed with ancillary competitions. In the Rookie Challenge, the Sophomores beat the Rookies 136-109. Cleveland’s Daniel Gibson earned MVP honors, scoring all 33 of his points on three-pointers—an outing that broke Kyle Korver’s 2005 record for most three-pointers in a single game. The Sophomores extended their winning streak to six.

Team San Antonio won the Three-Point Shootout, defeating Team Chicago in the final round. The squad featured Tim Duncan, David Robinson, and Becky Hammon. The victory came on a halfcourt shot made by Duncan.

Deron Williams claimed the Playstation Skills Challenge with a time of 25.5 seconds—fastest in the event’s history. He beat Chris Paul, who finished at 31.2 seconds. Dwyane Wade, who had won the past two years, was eliminated in the first round with a 53.9-second run. Jason Kidd also failed to advance, finishing at 39.7 seconds.

Jason Kapono of the Toronto Raptors won the Three-Point Shootout for the second year in a row, making him the first player since Peja Stojakovic (2002–2003) to do so. Kapono scored 25 points in the final, matching the record set by Mark Price and Craig Hodges in 1986. Daniel Gibson finished with 17 points, and Dirk Nowitzki, the 2006 champion, scored 14. Peja Stojakovic, Richard Hamilton, and Steve Nash were eliminated in the first round.

text:
Od arrived at Brenden Vetch’s farm not with fanfare, but quietly, as if she had simply stepped through the air, her presence more felt than announced. She was a giantess, yes, but not in the way legends describe—no booming voice, no rattle of armor. Her hands were stained with moss and root-traces. She carried no weapon, only a satchel of dried herbs and a scroll bound in leather that had seen more seasons than most men survive. She had vanished from Kelior centuries ago, after founding the city’s school of magic and healing its people from a blight that had killed half the population. No one knew where she’d gone. Now she stood on Brenden’s field, looking past the fence to his patch of moonlace and spindrift, plants he’d been tending since his brother died.

She invited him to Kelior. Not asked, not offered—invited, as though he were already part of a plan. He left the next morning. The journey took three weeks across the Blackfen, through the marshlands where the air hummed with dead voices, and up the River of Whispers. He expected a library, a spire, a place where fire could be shaped by will alone. Instead, he found a city built on silence. The streets were clean, the buildings symmetrical, but no one looked at him. No one spoke to him. The school existed, yes, but it was fenced behind iron gates, and the doors were locked.

The king ruled from a tower made of fused stone, and he wore robes not of silk but of woven light—practical, not ceremonial. His advisor, Valoren Greye, spoke in lists, not questions. He saw magic as a variable to be managed, not a force to be understood. To him, magic was not a language; it was a machine. He had banned the use of illusion, forbidden certain alchemical compounds, and punished anyone who tried to grow plants in the dark. Brenden had never met a magic user who saw it as a threat.

Princess Sulys sat at her father’s table but was not present. She had been promised to Valoren in a letter signed by her father, a man who had never spoken to her since her mother’s funeral. She had magic—something faint, a flicker beneath her skin when she touched soil—but they ignored it. They called it “improper energy,” “unstable.” She found Ceta Thiel in the archives, a woman who had spent ten years reading through old letters, star-charts, and soil samples from the northern wastes. Ceta believed Od had not died. She believed Od had left because the city had begun to fear her.

Yar Ayrwood, who worked in the school’s herb vaults, was one of Ceta’s sources. He was not a teacher, not officially, but he remembered songs Od used to sing to the roots. He sent his student, Elver, to the northern edge of the city, where the rocks wore patterns like faces. Elver returned with a stone that pulsed when held to the neck.

Valoren sent the warden, Arneth Pyt, to the Twilight Quarter, where a man named Tyramin performed nightly, his daughter Mistral dancing alongside him. The performance was real—the smoke, the light, the way the audience clapped after a spell made of wind and bone. But Valoren believed it was deception. He ordered Arneth to stop it. Arneth, however, was not clear on what was illusion and what was not. He watched Mistral’s hands move and felt the air shift. He began to doubt.

The king banned all public performances. Then Mistral asked for permission to perform at the palace. She stood before him, not in fear, but in certainty. She said, “I am not a threat.” Then she made the king’s crown float for three seconds. No one knew how.

Sulys stood up. She said, “I have magic. I’ve had it since I was seven. You ignored me. Now you want to erase it?” Her voice cracked, but not from fear.

That night, someone returned from the north. Brenden walked in with a pair of creatures made of stone and breath. Yar followed. And behind them, Elver—her face not her own, her voice not hushed, but clear.

Od had not died. She had changed. She had hidden. She had waited.

The king agreed to let the school operate without oversight. Magic was not to be controlled. It was not to be weaponized. It was to be allowed to grow.

text: In Japan, men who have sex with men (MSM) account for 78% of all male HIV cases reported in 2016, highlighting a significant disparity in infection rates. Over 30% of new HIV diagnoses in the country are made at the AIDS stage annually, suggesting many individuals remain unaware of their status for extended periods. An estimated two-thirds of Japanese MSM are not engaged with the gay community, yet most prior research has drawn samples from gay venues—potentially overlooking a large portion of the population. This study examined HIV testing behavior among MSM in Greater Tokyo who use mobile geo-social networking apps, platforms known to reach individuals not captured in traditional venue-based surveys. A total of 1,657 men were recruited through targeted ads on these apps. Lifetime HIV testing prevalence stood at 72.8%, while 29.7% had tested within the past six months. In multivariable models, higher lifetime testing was associated with older age, higher education, greater HIV knowledge, and engaging in anal intercourse with both regular and casual male partners. Attendance at gay venues also increased testing likelihood. Conversely, testing was lower among those who consistently use condoms with a regular partner, those who are married, those living outside central Tokyo, and those who have both male and female partners. These findings show that MSM using gay apps in Greater Tokyo fall short of CDC recommendations for annual HIV testing among high-risk groups. With limited prevention funding, moderate testing rates, and widespread app use, leveraging these platforms to promote nearby HIV testing services could be a cost-effective way to reach non-community-attached MSM, particularly younger men and those at higher risk for rapid disease progression.

text:
After earning his warrior name, Fireheart and Graystripe were sent to find the missing WindClan, scattered and clinging to life amid the tangle of Thunderpaths where the human roads met. They found them huddled near the broken edges of the machine-laid paths, starving, afraid. The Clan was brought back, though not whole—some had not survived the journey through the metal and noise.  

Not long after, Bluestar assigned Cinderpaw to Fireheart’s training, and Brackenpaw, Graystripe’s apprentice, to the same care. During a patrol along the river border, Graystripe darted after a vole across thin ice. The surface cracked beneath him. He plunged in, flailing, nearly swallowed by the cold rush. Silverstream, a RiverClan warrior, pulled him out. The two had been near each other before, but now something shifted—something immediate and undeniable. They met again at the river’s edge, then later at the edge of the clearing, always under the moon. The bond was forbidden, but it grew, not from choice, but from the weight of what they could not stop.  

Fireheart tried to speak to them. He said the warrior code was not a suggestion. But his warnings only made them more desperate to keep their secret. In the end, Graystripe agreed to meet only at the Gathering, under the open sky where all Clans could see, but not where they could stop it.  

Tigerclaw was watching. He had long wanted Bluestar’s place. He laid a trap on the Thunderpath, aiming to kill her and clear his path. The trap caught Cinderpaw instead. She survived, but her hind leg was ruined—she would never run fast enough to fight, never leap to the top of a tree. Yellowfang took her as her apprentice, not for her strength, but for her patience. She learned to read the signs in bark and leaf, to quiet the body when the mind was loud.  

Fireheart found his sister, Princess, in a Twolegplace where the air tasted of smoke and stale food. She was a kittypet once, now a cat of the human world, but not broken by it. She brought her youngest, Cloudkit, to the forest. He had the same green eyes as Fireheart, not from blood, but from the way he looked at the trees. Bluestar allowed him to stay. Brindleface took him in, not as a warrior, but as a cat who needed to learn how to be still.  

The old wounds were not buried. Brokenstar, exiled and broken, returned with others who had been cast out. He led them in a raid. The fight was sharp, close. Yellowfang fought him, clawed his eyes out. He was left blind, not dead, not forgiven. He was locked in the hollow beneath the elders’ den.  

Then RiverClan and ShadowClan turned on WindClan. The clash erupted at the border, not over territory, but over hunger. Fireheart was knocked down by Leopardfur, RiverClan’s deputy. He was alone. Tigerclaw stood near, watching. He did nothing.  

Later, Silverstream came to Fireheart, not to ask for anything, but to say she knew what he felt—what he had to choose. Fireheart did not touch her. He saw Graystripe shaking, not from fear, but from knowing. Darkstripe saw. He told Tigerclaw. Tigerclaw said nothing. But he listened.  

After that, Fireheart stopped believing in loyalty. He had seen it. He had seen it fail. He had seen what it cost to be honest when power was the only truth left.

text:
Cadel Piggot is taken to a psychologist as a child not because he’s ill, but because he thinks too fast—his hands move before his thoughts settle, and machines respond to him as if he’s spoken to them. He doesn’t play like other kids. He bypasses instructions, rewires systems, and sees through the lies built into everyday things. His mind doesn’t lag; it leaps ahead, leaving others behind. The people around him don’t understand him, and he doesn’t understand why they flinch when he speaks. He doesn’t mean to disrupt. He just sees how things work—and how they break.

Phineas Darkkon appears in his life like a rumor, a name attached to a voice on a monitor. He claims to be Cadel’s father. Later, the man who treats him—the psychologist named Thaddeus Roth—turns out to be Prosper English, a former associate of Darkkon’s, who also says he’s Cadel’s father. No one tells Cadel to doubt them. No one tells him to question.

At the Axis Institute, Cadel learns to hack, to infiltrate, to move through networks like a ghost. He’s given no rules, only access. He builds systems, then dismantles them. The world he touches—online, in terminals, in the rhythms of data—starts to fray. People stop speaking to each other. Devices fail. Systems collapse, not from error, but because Cadel sees a flaw and fixes it by breaking something else.

Then, a girl walks into his life. She moves slowly, her hand trembling as she opens a door. He doesn’t know her name. He doesn’t know she has cerebral palsy. But she watches him. She doesn’t flinch when he speaks too fast. She doesn’t ask him to stop. When he breaks a program and watches it spiral, she says, “You don’t have to fix everything.” That’s when he begins to hear, not the machine, but the silence between the signals.

Mstislav Los, a man who worked alone in a rusted workshop outside Kazan, built a pulse detonation rocket from scavenged parts and half-remembered equations. He didn’t speak much, and when he did, it was about fuel ratios or magnetic confinement. In 1924, he found Alexei Gusev, a retired artillery officer with a scar across his left cheek, sitting on a broken bench in a vacant lot. Gusev had stopped believing in anything but gravity. They launched together.

The journey took eighteen months. When they landed near Valles Marineris, the atmosphere was thin but breathable. The city was built into the crust—tunnels lined with coolant pipes and rusted conduits, workers moving in shifts beneath a sky choked with dust. The ruling class called themselves Engineers. Toscoob, their head, stood in a chamber lined with dead projectors and said the city had to be burned to stop its decay. His daughter, Aelita, found Los in a storage alcove. She spoke in a flat, precise voice. The ice caps hadn’t melted in two decades. The planet was dying.

Gusev tried to rally the workers. Los watched. He didn’t join. He stood in a courtyard after the uprising failed, listening to the silence that followed the last explosion. They fled in a scrap-hulled skimmer. Earth received their signal three years later. The transmission was faint—just a name, repeated. *Los*. Then static.

Tuesday brought no relief to the Khadr family. They waited through hours of legal motion and judicial review, knowing the outcome would shape Abdullah’s future for months to come. He had been held for nearly four years, detained on allegations he helped Afghan militants obtain weapons. The court’s decision followed a pattern: it echoed a 2005 ruling that denied his release pending extradition to the U.S., where he faces federal conspiracy charges.

Abdullah’s grandparents, Fatmah and Mohammad Elsamnah, offered their Toronto home—valued at $300,000—as bond. The house was meant to serve as collateral, a promise of responsibility if he were released. But the judge rejected the arrangement after questioning Mohammad, whose speech was halting, difficult to follow, and marked by gaps in memory. The court found him unable to fulfill the role of guardian.

The family’s legal team pointed to support from the Salaheddin Islamic Centre, where Abdullah’s family has worshipped. In response, the mosque raised $50,000 for supervision, agreed to fund an ankle monitor with GPS tracking, and offered Abdullah a position. The mosque’s manager also committed to daily transportation. Crown lawyers Matthew Sullivan and Howard Piafsky challenged the mosque’s credibility, querying RCMP officer Tarek Mokdad about any known ties between worshippers and militant activity.

Justice Trotter ruled out any connection between the mosque and terrorism. Still, he declared the donations improper because they were made without expectation of return, regardless of Abdullah’s future behavior. The court did not accept the gift as a condition of release.

Abdullah learned the verdict only after calling his family on Wednesday evening. He had not been told during the hearing.

text: This book traces the development of creationism from the moment Darwin’s ideas challenged established views. It opens with the immediate pushback Darwin’s theory of evolution met, then follows George Frederick Wright as he moves from accepting Darwin’s framework to rejecting it, aligning instead with the emerging Fundamentalist movement. The account then turns to the rift between Fundamentalists and Modernists, highlighting the role of William Jennings Bryan in shaping the debate. It details how two self-taught figures—Harry Rimmer and George McCready Price—used amateur science to defend a literal reading of Genesis. The mid-20th century brings the formation of groups like the Religion and Science Association and the Deluge Geology Society, while the American Scientific Affiliation began to embrace theistic evolution. Resistance to this shift emerged in force, spearheaded by Henry M. Morris and John C. Whitcomb, Jr., whose 1961 book *The Genesis Flood* became a cornerstone of the new creationist effort. Their work led to the founding of the Creation Research Society and the broader creation science movement. Morris later established the Institute for Creation Research, while the Seventh-day Adventist Church created the Geoscience Research Institute to advance its own geological stance. The book ends with an examination of how creationist ideas took root in churches across the U.S. and beyond, and how, in later decades, the intelligent design movement began to supplant earlier forms.

text: A terrestrial laser scanner captures detailed forest structure quickly and with high accuracy, and its use in forest inventory research has expanded steadily. This study introduces BEE, an automated, low-cost scanner developed by the Department of Electronic Engineering at Beijing Forestry University. At its core is a SICK LMS-511 two-dimensional laser sensor and a stepper motor, designed specifically for 3D scanning of individual trees. The system runs custom software that controls operations and records angular positions, range measurements, and intensity values. Raw data are transformed into point clouds, range maps, and intensity maps. From a single scan per plot, the software identifies trees and fits a local ground plane for each. Using these, it estimates diameter at breast height (DBH), height, and position automatically. The scanner was tested in a planted ginkgo stand in Haidian District, Beijing, across four 10 m × 10 m plots. Data were collected from one scan per plot, and results were compared to manual measurements. Tree trunk detection succeeded in 92.75% of cases across all plots. For DBH, the root mean square error (RMSE) was 1.27 cm; for height, it was 0.24 m. Estimated tree positions aligned closely with actual field locations. Further testing occurred in JiuFeng Forest Park, where two 5-meter-radius plots were scanned. In the flat plot, eleven trees were detected and their DBH estimated successfully. In the plot with uneven terrain, detection failed entirely. These results show that BEE can accurately estimate key structural parameters in managed forest stands and offer a viable path for field deployment in forest inventory, particularly under controlled or uniform conditions.

text:
The EPA oversees the asbestos cleanup in Libby, Montana, a town on the Superfund National Priorities List since 2002. Contamination from asbestos has been a persistent issue there for more than a decade. The problem traces back to the early 1900s, when the Zonolite Company mined vermiculite in the region, a material that naturally contained tremolite asbestos. W.R. Grace & Company operated the mine from 1963 until 1990. The Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry reported that residents of Libby face higher rates of asbestosis than the national average.

Inhaling airborne asbestos fibers leads to serious health effects: mesothelioma, lung scarring, asbestosis, and lung cancer. These conditions typically develop after years of exposure. Mesothelioma, which forms in the lining of the lungs, abdomen, or heart, carries a grim outlook—most diagnosed individuals survive only six months to a year.

Asbestos dust from the mine began escaping into the air as early as 1919, spreading through residential areas, vehicles, and public spaces. At times, the dust was thick enough to resemble a sandstorm, coating surfaces and raising concerns about everyday exposure.

After Grace & Company ended operations, they admitted that the vermiculite they processed contained asbestos. The company said they implemented corrective actions after the mine closed. As part of settlement agreements, Grace & Company committed $250 million from a total $333 million allocation by the EPA and the Department of Health and Human Services. This money will fund medical care and environmental cleanup over five years. It does not cover all past medical expenses incurred by Libby and Troy residents.

text:
In Philadelphia, 14-year-old Matilda Cook, called Mattie, lives above the family’s coffeehouse with her mother, her grandfather—a veteran of the Revolutionary War—and Eliza, a formerly enslaved woman who works as their cook. Mattie has always believed the coffeehouse could become something more, a place where people gathered not just for coffee but for conversation, for change. But in the summer of 1793, that future shatters with the arrival of yellow fever.

The city grows quiet at first, then desperate. Neighbors vanish. The streets fill with the sound of carts hauling bodies. Mattie watches as Polly, their serving girl, falls ill and dies within days. Then her mother. Mattie and her grandfather try to escape to a relative’s farm in the countryside, but guards stop them at the city’s edge. They see her grandfather coughing and assume he’s infected. They turn him away. The decision sticks in Mattie’s chest like a splinter.

She falls ill soon after, her body wracked with fever. Her grandfather takes her to a hospital—then returns to the empty house, only to find it ransacked. The next night, men break in. In the dark, they fight. Mattie’s grandfather doesn’t survive.

She wakes alone in the house, fever-broken, the air thick with silence and smoke. She finds Eliza, who has been hiding. Together, they scavenge for supplies, tend to the sick. They take in Nell, a girl who lost her parents to the fever. Eliza’s two nephews arrive, coughing blood. Mattie and Eliza bring them to the coffeehouse, close the shutters, and wait.

There is no cure. Medicine does nothing. The city is dead. Then, one morning, frost lies across the cobblestones. The mosquitoes stop biting. The fever ends.

Mattie’s mother, Lucille, returns from the countryside, weak but alive. She is with the President, who has come to assess the city’s recovery. Mattie stands in the doorway of the coffeehouse, watching her mother walk in. The place is scarred—walls cracked, windows boarded, the counter stained with old coffee and blood. But it is still standing.

She looks at Eliza. She says nothing. But she begins to work. The coffeehouse will stay open. Not for memory. Not for pity. For the next person who needs to sit down, and not be afraid.

text:
August 1949. Ndotsheni, a village nestled in the South African countryside near Ixopo. The Rev. Stephen Kumalo, priest of St. Mark’s Church, gets word from his brother John in Johannesburg: their sister is in trouble. He leaves the village the next day, not just to help her but to find Absalom, his son, who’s been working the gold mines. The journey takes him through dust and heat, into the city’s grim sprawl.  

In Johannesburg, he finds his sister, but she won’t leave her life behind. She asks him to take care of her son, Alex. Stephen spends days searching. He finds Absalom in a small room, newly released from jail. His son says he and two friends are planning a robbery—there’s no other way out, he says. He’s been offered a chance to escape the mines, but he knows it’s not real. His girlfriend, Irina, is pregnant. She begs him not to go. He listens, but still goes.  

The robbery happens in the dark. They break into a house. During the struggle, Absalom shoots Arthur Jarvis, a white man, a friend of Stephen’s. Jarvis had been at the door when the shot rang out.  

Absalom is arrested. Stephen stands in the courtroom, stunned, unable to speak. His son confesses. The two others lie, swear they didn’t see anything, and walk free. Absalom says he did it. He says he knew it was wrong. He says he was afraid. He’s sentenced to death.  

Stephen performs a wedding in prison. He marries Absalom and Irina, not in celebration, but as a way to hold on to something. Afterward, he returns to Ndotsheni with Irina and Alex.  

The village is quiet. Alex plays near the homestead. The infant son of Arthur Jarvis, born just weeks after the shooting, lies in a cradle not far away. They don’t speak, not yet. But they touch hands once, and again.  

Stephen tells the congregation he can no longer serve. No one argues. The church holds its breath.  

On the morning of the execution, the sky is gray. No wind. The clock ticks slowly. Stephen sits alone on the porch. At four o’clock, a man arrives. He wears a black coat. He doesn’t shout. He doesn’t cry. He says he’s Arthur Jarvis’s father. He says he knows what it means to lose a son. He reaches out. Stephen takes his hand. Neither man speaks.

text:
Continuing to pour resources into a failing plan—what is often called the sunk-cost fallacy—reveals a pattern where people act against clear economic logic. Past investments are gone, irrecoverable, yet the emotional weight of them persists. Rational choice theory holds that decisions should depend only on future prospects, not on what has already been lost. Yet in practice, people often double down on failing courses of action.

This study examines whether the fallacy stems from emotions generated by the decision itself—integral affect—rather than fleeting emotional states unrelated to the situation. In Study 1, participants’ immediate emotional reactions to a failing investment scenario predicted their willingness to continue funding it. Study 2 used a within-subjects design to confirm this link. When participants considered a scenario where they had to decide whether to invest further, their emotional responses directly shaped their choices. The effect vanished when the same scenarios were presented without the investment choice, showing the emotional response was tied to the decision, not incidental mood.

Study 3 repeated these results and added a new layer: those who had to justify their initial decision were less likely to continue investing, and reported less negative emotion when faced with the failure. The act of providing a reason seemed to dampen the emotional pull. Study 4 tested whether mental effort matters. Under high cognitive load—when people had less capacity for deliberate thought—the link between emotional response and continued investment grew stronger. This suggests that when people can’t think carefully, they rely more on gut feelings, which amplifies the bias.

The findings point to integral emotional responses as the core driver. Justification and cognitive load act as modulators—justification reduces the effect, cognitive strain increases it. The pattern is not about regret or blame, but about how emotionally charged a decision feels in the moment. Interventions that encourage deliberate reasoning and prompt people to justify choices may help reduce this bias.

text:
Theresa meets Tony through a friend’s arrangement, a setup meant to feel casual but carries the quiet weight of expectation. The first conversation stumbles—awkward, halting—but then a thread emerges: both grew up in small towns in Iowa. For a moment, there’s something real. Then the ease fractures. He asks too many questions about her routine, watches her too long. She ends the date quietly, not out of anger, but because the space between them feels less like intimacy and more like pressure.

He doesn’t stop. He shows up at her office building without warning, waits outside. His calls at home are short—just her name, then silence. She tells her coworker, who listens, says nothing. She calls the police. Officer Beck reviews the file, nods, offers no solution, only a suggestion: leave. Change your name. Move.

She tries to keep going—to work, to small rituals—but the fear settles deep. After months, she vanishes. No forwarding address. No messages. She shows up in Denver under a new name, living in a rented room with a view of a parking lot. Her old life is not erased—it’s buried. Tony’s reach isn’t physical anymore, but it’s everywhere—like a quiet hum beneath the world. She’s no longer a person with choices. She’s a pattern of survival.

text:
Last Saturday, an 8.8 magnitude earthquake shook Chile, triggering a tsunami that surged over Pichilemu’s shoreline. The waves hit without warning, sweeping through the coastal district and leveling much of the costanera, with floodwaters spilling into the city square. Pichilemu, known in Mapudungun as "small forest," is a central Chilean resort town celebrated for its surf break at Punta de Lobos. Though the town’s core escaped major structural harm from the quake, the tsunami devastated the waterfront. Fishermen Creek, a coastal industrial zone, was wiped out—its machinery buried under debris. The Agustín Ross architecture that defines the area, including three National Monuments, suffered serious damage. The Agustín Ross Mirador, a landmark promenade near Fishermen Creek, collapsed entirely; its iron railings vanished in the surge. Restaurants, beach kiosks, and even the old circus pavilion were swept away.

In surrounding rural zones—Ciruelos, Rodeillo, Espinillo—many adobe homes, some more than a century old, were reduced to rubble or left unfit to live in.

The strongest aftershock, recorded at 03:10 local time (07:10 UTC) on March 2, struck about 40 kilometers offshore, measuring 5.5 on the Richter scale per USGS data. 

In response, Intendant Juan Núñez convened with Governor Loreto Puebla, Mayor Roberto Córdova, military and naval commanders, and neighborhood council representatives. They agreed to send Carabineros forces into Pichilemu to maintain order.

text: In 1859, John Deane, twelve years old, lived in Gettysburg with his family. He spent much of his time with Nicholas, a Black boy who worked in their home, teaching him to break in a young colt. John was shoved into the cellar and left there for days. He was freed by a cook from the Union camp—a man he’d once shared bread with, whom he’d assumed was just a servant. After that, he enlisted in the Union Army and stayed through to the war’s end.

text: Fred Barber, an American tourist, stepped onto a quiet estate in the English countryside during the Second World War. He didn’t mean to break anything—just poured a bottle of whiskey into the stone bowl meant for milk, a sacred offering left for the fairies. The next morning, he woke not in his rented room, but on a mossy bank beneath a sky the color of tarnished silver. He was taken by the very presence he’d disturbed, not as punishment, but as a replacement: a child had vanished from a cradle, and Barber was sent in its place. The Land of Faerie unfolded around him—not as legend, but as a place where the rules had frayed, where promises could unravel like thread, and where truth had no fixed shape. He traveled westward, through forests that shifted at night, toward the court of Oberon, not to claim a crown, but to prove he had once been human. The path didn’t end where it began. It ended in something else entirely—something he hadn’t known to fear, or to hope for.

text:
Among 1,005 healthy Portuguese students sampled in April 2016, paired oropharyngeal swabs (OPS) and saliva samples were collected, stored at –80°C, and analyzed using direct qPCR and culture-based PCR. The goal was to improve detection of Neisseria meningitidis (Nm) carriage, particularly in young people, where reliable surveillance is critical for assessing vaccine impact. Standard culture methods have previously shown limited sensitivity, prompting this evaluation of alternative approaches.

Of the 460 saliva samples that met evaluation criteria, 36.1% were positive for Nm via direct qPCR targeting sodC. This exceeded the 12.5% positivity rate from OPS samples (126 positives). When culture-amplified PCR was applied, 94 saliva samples tested positive—more than the OPS results, but still fewer than direct qPCR. The increase suggests culture supplementation enhances recovery, especially for low-abundance or stressed organisms. Viable Nm was recovered from saliva in multiple cases, confirming the sample’s viability for pathogen detection.

Additional qPCR assays targeted specific Nm genes (sodC), genogroup-specific loci (B, C, W, X, Y), and porA from cultured isolates, with cycle threshold ≤36 defining positivity. Overall, Nm carriage was 36.1% across all sample types, with encapsulated Nm (including MenB) detected in 5.5%. OPS-only direct qPCR identified Nm in 12.5% and MenB in 2.2%.

Notably, current MenB carriage (2.9%) was significantly lower than in a prior survey four years earlier (6.8%), a shift with p = 0.0003. The results indicate that combining saliva and OPS sampling with both direct and culture-amplified PCR improves sensitivity. This integrated approach offers a stronger foundation for tracking changes in Nm carriage and transmission, particularly in youth, where vaccine effects are most relevant.

Three tornadoes touched down in western Massachusetts on Wednesday, confirmed by the National Weather Service’s Taunton office. The strongest, rated EF-3 on the Enhanced Fujita scale, originated in Westfield and traveled 63 kilometers (39 miles) across the region. Its passage killed four and left 200 injured. In West Springfield, the storm peeled roofs from buildings and triggered partial structural failures. As it crossed the Connecticut River into Springfield—the state’s third-largest city—it destroyed dozens of homes and severely damaged commercial properties along the city’s south side. The tornado weakened near Charlton and finally ended, with damage documented in over 19 communities.

Massachusetts Governor Deval Patrick activated a state of emergency and deployed 1,000 National Guard personnel to support recovery efforts. Reports of looting have surfaced in several impacted zones. Two other tornadoes, both EF-1, touched down in Wilbraham and North Brimfield. The North Brimfield tornado lasted 1.3 miles, while the one in Wilbraham covered 3.6 miles. Although tornadoes are uncommon in New England, they are not unheard of. In 1953, a deadly F-4 tornado struck Worcester—the state’s second-largest city—burning for 80 minutes and killing more than 90 people, one of the deadliest tornado events in U.S. history.

Jacen Solo walks the dark side now, not as a man caught in a choice, but as one who has settled into the rhythm of it. He calls himself Darth Caedus, not in mockery, not in pride, but as a name that fits. He believes the galaxy cannot hold itself together without a hand that does not flinch. That belief has become a blade that cuts deeper with every action. He no longer weighs the cost of lives—friendships, blood, the quiet hopes of strangers. He sees only the shape of order, and if it requires a body on the ground, a family scattered, a city burned to ash, then it is done.

Tenel Ka was his lover once. He made her believe he was different. When she learned the truth—that he ordered the massacre of a wookiee village to break a resistance, that he let a child die to prove a point—her trust snapped. She turned on him, not with fury, but with quiet finality, as if she had been waiting for the moment to walk away. Jaina, his sister, died not in battle, but on his command. He sent her to a trap she did not see, and when she reached for the truth, he let her fall.

The only ones left are those he has shaped. Tahiri Veila still follows him, not because she believes in his cause, but because he made her remember her brother’s death, and twisted that memory into loyalty. Anakin Solo, her lover, stays close, not out of affection, but because Caedus has made him afraid to move.

The violence escalates. He approves strikes on civilian centers on Kashyyyk, not as strategy, but as demonstration. He watches reports of dead children and does not blink. When one of his own agents in the Corellian government nearly exposes a plot, Caedus does not hesitate. He orders the execution not for security, but because he wants to show that no one is safe if they speak too freely. Fear becomes a currency he spends freely.

He attacks the Jedi Praxeum on Ossus. His forces storm the compound. He watches the recordings of the slaughter, the bodies of adult Jedi stacked in corridors. He sees Jaina die, not in combat, but in a hallway, her lightsaber still active, her face frozen in disbelief. He wants the children. Not to train them. To own them.

He manipulates Tenel Ka into surrendering her last fleet. She gives it up, thinking she is saving her daughter. She does not know how easily he has already marked her as weak. The coup comes quick after. She is left with nothing.

He pressures Ben Skywalker to kill Cal Omas. He tells Coruscant he knows of an attack, knowing Ben will act. When Ben refuses, Caedus locks him in a chamber beneath the Senate Tower. He does not ask for obedience. He wants to break him. The torture is long, not for information, but for transformation.

Luke arrives. He finds Ben bleeding, half-conscious, his face hollowed by pain. He does not draw his blade at first. He sees the moment when Ben still has a choice. He steps in. A fight follows. Luke does not kill him. Not yet.

Meanwhile, on Korriban, a signal stirs. A ship—Ship, the one Ben recovered from Ziost—has not been silent. Its logs, buried in old Sith protocols, hint at a network older than Caedus, deeper than any name he has spoken. It may outlive him. No one knows if it will rise. But it is still there.

text: A gradient-based analytical method, initially developed for resting-state fMRI, revealed a core organizational axis in the cerebral cortex—running from primary sensory-motor regions to transmodal association areas. This approach has now been adapted to cerebellar imaging, identifying two dominant functional gradients within the cerebellum for the first time. Gradient 1 maps a shift from motor control regions to areas overlapping with the default-mode network. Gradient 2 separates regions engaged in focused task processing from those more involved in internal mentation. The study introduces LittleBrain, an open-source toolbox built to interpret cerebellar neuroimaging data through this topographical framework. It projects all cerebellar voxels onto a two-dimensional scatterplot, with each axis aligned to one of the two functional gradients. This representation captures continuous functional variation across the cerebellum, revealing subtler patterns than discrete parcellation schemes allow. By visualizing activation maps, volumetric data, and task-related responses in this space, LittleBrain makes it possible to see how functional shifts unfold across the cerebellar surface. The tool is freely accessible at https://xaviergp.github.io/littlebrain, supporting straightforward integration into cerebellar fMRI workflows.

text: We modeled how hostility shifts between individuals after a major cultural threat, like a terrorist attack, drawing on Terror Management Theory and Social Judgement Theory. Each agent holds a cultural identity defined by acceptance ranges for three worldviews: Atheist, Muslim, and Christian. Agents assess others by comparing cultural identities—how close or distant their positions are. When an attack occurs in the name of an extreme Muslim identity, agents who perceive themselves as targeted by that extremist view tend to shrink their acceptance range for Muslim identity. It emerges from the structure of cultural identities within each population—how tightly or loosely held positions are, and how clearly boundaries are drawn. These patterns are explained by the internal configuration of identity acceptance ranges, not by external labels or assumptions.

text:
Five teenagers—Olivia, Mo, Charlie, Stella, and Wen—end up in detention for different reasons. The room is quiet except for the hum of the fluorescent lights and the occasional rustle of paper. Then, a jingle cuts through the silence on a radio someone left on. Olivia starts humming, then sings. Mo joins in, then Charlie, Stella, and Wen. No one plans it. The song isn’t polished, but it’s there—something real, something unforced. They keep going.

They begin playing together at lunch, in empty classrooms, in the basement of Olivia’s house. At first, they argue over rhythm, volume, tone—what kind of music they want to make. But over time, the arguments fade. Not because they agree, but because they stop trying to change each other. They start noticing the way Mo’s voice fits under Charlie’s guitar, how Stella’s trumpet adds a sharpness to Olivia’s lyrics, how Wen’s drumming finds a pulse even when the others falter.

They decide to play at the school’s Halloween Bash. The announcement spreads fast. So does the backlash. Mudslide Crush, the band everyone’s been talking about, has a following. Ray, a Mudslide Crush member and someone who’s made life difficult for Olivia since she started walking the halls alone, shows up at the school’s music office. He tells Olivia her band won’t fit in. He calls her music “noise,” says she’s not good enough. Mo steps in. Then Charlie. Then Stella. She grabs a cup of lemonade from the cafeteria line and throws it straight at Ray’s face. It lands on his shirt, his glasses, his jacket. He stumbles back. Someone says, “Lemonade Mouth.” It sticks.

The school removes the lemonade machine the next week. It’s gone by Friday morning. The principal says it’s to make room for a new gym, funded by a sports drink company. The band members feel the shift—something official, cold, replacing something that was theirs.

On the night of the Bash, they walk on stage. No one expects them. The opening riff is a trumpet line from Stella, then a ukulele from Wen, a rhythm from Mo, and Olivia’s voice. It isn’t perfect. But it’s not trying to be. The crowd doesn’t cheer at first. Then, someone starts clapping. Then another. The room fills.

After Olivia’s cat dies, they go to her house. No one says much. They sit on the floor. Mo brings a blanket. Charlie plays a slow tune on his guitar. Stella says she once thought she was stupid. Wen says he doesn’t know how to talk to his father about his new wife. text: Four hundred forty individuals were recruited online and assigned to one of three conditions: a health-literate action plan using guided implementation intentions, a standard action plan with self-directed implementation intentions, or an education control using a fact-sheet on healthy snacking. Health literacy was assessed using the Newest Vital Sign (NVS), revealing that 52% had adequate literacy, 24% had low, and 25% had possibly low levels. While no overall difference emerged between groups, a significant interaction between health literacy level and intervention type was found (b = 1.7, p = 0.03). For participants scoring two points below the NVS mean (M = 3.4, SD = 2.0), the health-literate action plan led to 8 fewer weekly servings of unhealthy snacks compared to the standard action plan. Among those scoring two points above the mean, the health-literate plan was associated with 6 more weekly servings of unhealthy snacks relative to the standard plan. These findings suggest that identical intervention formats may not serve all users equally. Tailoring behavioral support to health literacy levels—especially for those with lower literacy—could improve outcomes. ANZCTR identifier: ACTRN12617001194358.

text:
Heavy episodic drinking among college students remains a persistent concern, prompting closer examination of what predicts such behavior. This study tested whether implicit associations with alcohol, self-control capacity, and their interplay could forecast actual drinking in a lab environment. Previous work suggested self-control might shape how strongly implicit alcohol links predict consumption, but this research pushed further by using a validated manipulation: participants completed either a more or less cognitively taxing task, followed by an incentive designed to encourage restraint. The design incorporated multiple established assessments—three Implicit Association Tests measuring drinking identity, alcohol excite, and alcohol approach, alongside their explicit versions—to capture both automatic and conscious associations.

The main expectation was that under higher cognitive load, implicit alcohol associations would show a stronger link to actual drinking. A secondary focus examined whether individual differences in mental resources—specifically implicit beliefs about willpower and measured working memory capacity—would alter that dynamic. One hundred five U.S. undergraduate heavy episodic drinkers provided baseline data on drinking habits, implicit and explicit alcohol associations, beliefs about willpower, and working memory performance. After random assignment to task difficulty condition, participants completed their assigned task, received the drinking incentive, and then took part in a controlled alcohol taste test.

The results did not support the hypothesis. The manipulation failed to produce a detectable difference in perceived cognitive demand, and no significant interaction emerged between implicit alcohol associations and task load. The absence of a moderating effect challenges assumptions about how automatic associations and self-control jointly influence drinking under lab conditions. These findings suggest that implicit measures may not reliably predict consumption in controlled settings, or that the conditions for meaningful interaction between implicit processes and self-regulation remain poorly understood.

The novel opens in 2007 with a U.S. military incursion into Turkey, driven by strategic interest in borax deposits critical to advanced electronics and energy infrastructure. American forces quickly seize control of major urban centers, then attempt to reinstate the Treaty of Sèvres—a historical agreement that had dissolved the Ottoman Empire—by carving Turkey between Greece and Armenia, two former antagonists. Turkey resists. In response, Ankara forms a defensive alliance with China, Russia, and Germany, pooling intelligence and military assets. The turning point comes when a Turkish operative, embedded within U.S. intelligence operations, extracts a portable nuclear warhead from a secure U.S. facility. The device is detonated in downtown Washington, D.C. The blast kills millions, collapses key government infrastructure, and shatters public confidence in the U.S. command structure.

Instead of halting the campaign, the U.S. escalates. Occupation forces intensify their control over captured cities, imposing harsh curfews, mass detentions, and systematic suppression of dissent. When U.S. troops enter Istanbul, the city becomes a battleground. Fighting erupts between American units, remnants of the Turkish Armed Forces, local police, and armed civilians. The urban conflict is not cinematic—there are no large-scale charges or heroic last stands, only scattered engagements, sniping from rooftops, and buildings reduced to rubble.

The real shift comes not from battlefield outcomes but from geopolitical reaction. The destruction of Washington, combined with the U.S. occupation’s brutality, triggers a coordinated response. Russia, the European Union, and China activate a joint military coordination framework. They issue a formal warning: further U.S. advances will trigger mutually assured destruction. The U.S. government, already weakened by internal fractures, withdraws its forces. Turkey is liberated, though not restored to its pre-invasion state.

The operative responsible for the Washington strike belongs to "The Grey Team," a clandestine unit composed of children recruited as infants and raised under absolute obedience and ideological detachment. After neutralizing the invasion’s financial architect—a billionaire CEO who also funds the U.S. President—they take him into custody. The final scene depicts the CEO subjected to prolonged, methodical interrogation, not for information, but for symbolic reckoning. The U.S. administration in the narrative mirrors George W. Bush’s presidency, marked by evangelical rhetoric, military overreach, and a close-knit inner circle including figures modeled on Condoleezza Rice and Donald Rumsfeld. The novel includes real political figures from that era, portrayed in roles consistent with their public profiles.

A video system using eight synchronized cameras captured a hip resurfacing surgery from multiple angles, designed to overcome the spatial limitations of traditional single-camera surgical videos. The procedure was performed by an experienced attending surgeon. Thirty medical students were randomly assigned to either the multiple POV group (experimental) or the single POV group (control). Before viewing, all participants took a knowledge test. After watching their assigned video, they completed a simulated pin insertion into the femoral head, using the video as a guide. Post-simulation, they took a second knowledge test and filled out a Likert-scale questionnaire.

Performance was measured against the pre-operative plan. The experimental group showed a 29% reduction in angular deviation during pin placement (p = 0.037), while entry point accuracy did not differ significantly (p = 0.204). Two orthopedic attendings assessed performance using a modified global rating scale; the experimental group scored 3.5% higher (p = 0.046). Knowledge gains were substantially greater in the experimental group—32% higher than control (p < 0.001)—and self-reported confidence improved by 21% (p = 0.002). Baseline knowledge levels were not significantly different between groups (p = 0.721).

The findings suggest that multi-angle video recording enhances precision in surgical planning and improves both self-assessed and expert-rated skill acquisition. This approach offers a measurable advantage in learning complex orthopedic procedures, particularly when spatial understanding is critical.

text: After his father died, Anton Wohlfart began work as an apprentice in T. O. Schröter’s Breslau trading office. He earned his place through steady effort, not luck. Over time, he moved from clerking to handling accounts, then to managing shipments—each step bringing him closer to a stable life as a minor bourgeois. He spent years in the Schröter office, forming quiet ties with the family, and once or twice a year, dined at Rothsattel manor. That world faded when the estate was liquidated in 1823, the sale marked by cold arithmetic, not mourning. He met Veitel Itzig again in 1821, an old acquaintance from Ostrau, now a banker in Berlin. Herr von Fink, one of Schröter’s partners, remained a name on correspondence, a man with a scar near his left ear, who never forgot a debt—and never forgave one either.

text:
The European Union and Canada have imposed a 15% tariff on select U.S. imports, backed by a World Trade Organization ruling. The move follows a longstanding dispute over the Byrd Amendment, a U.S. law that redirects funds collected from foreign companies found to have dumped goods into the American market—money previously used to support domestic industries. The WTO declared the amendment illegal in September 2002, citing violations of international trade norms. Despite that, the U.S. Congress failed to repeal it, leaving the door open for retaliatory measures.

As of May 1st, the EU has targeted paper products, textile goods, and industrial machinery. Canada’s response includes live swine, cigarettes, and oysters. The financial impact on affected U.S. firms has already materialized: Timken and Lancaster Colony Corp. have received payments under the amendment’s framework. The EU estimates that if the law remains in effect, it could pay out up to $1.6 billion in the next fiscal year. The U.S. Congressional Budget Office projects a similar figure—about $1.15 billion—for the year after.

The EU tariffs are expected to generate roughly $26 million in revenue; Canada’s will produce about $11.6 million. Japan and Mexico are reviewing similar actions. President Bush has urged Congress to repeal the amendment since February, but no legislative action has occurred. The outcome remains pending.

A new outbreak of E. coli O157:H7 has been linked to fresh bagged spinach sold in at least twenty U.S. states. Federal and state health agencies report one fatality—a 77-year-old woman from Wisconsin—and 95 confirmed cases of illness. Patients range in age from three to 84. The most serious complications include hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS), which has affected children and older adults, and acute kidney failure, documented in at least fourteen individuals. Common symptoms include bloody diarrhea and low-grade fever.

Authorities emphasize that washing spinach will not remove the bacteria. Consumers are instructed to throw out all bagged spinach, regardless of brand or packaging, and avoid using any that might have been part of the contaminated batch. While cooking the product would likely destroy the pathogen, officials advise against consuming any affected items due to the risk of exposure during handling.

The investigation points to Natural Selection Foods LLC, a California producer that supplies multiple brands—Dole, Trader Joe’s, Earthbound Farm, Rave Spinach, and its private-label items—as a likely source. The company has pulled all spinach products from distribution. However, officials warn that contamination may have come from other suppliers, and the root cause remains under active review.

E. coli O157:H7 infections cause roughly 75,000 cases annually in the United States, with severe outcomes possible in up to 60 people each year. Health officials expect new cases to emerge as the investigation continues, but most patients are projected to recover within a week.

A Spanish civil guard was killed and another seriously wounded in a shooting in Capbreton, a town on France’s southwest coast, just after 8:30 a.m. UTC. Sepsis patients in the emergency department often need more than the standard 5mg/kg dose of gentamicin to reach therapeutic peak concentrations. This study focused on identifying the minimum effective dose to achieve target levels—specifically, a peak concentration of at least 16mg/L, ideally 20mg/L—given that a peak/MIC ratio of 8–10 is considered essential for optimal bactericidal effect.

Data from August 2015 to February 2017 included 86 ED sepsis patients. After the first 5mg/kg dose, peak levels were measured 30 minutes later. Only 44% of patients reached 16mg/L, and just 15% achieved 20mg/L. The analysis then simulated higher dosing. A 7mg/kg dose predicted that 96.5% would exceed 16mg/L and 77.9% would surpass 20mg/L.

In the final phase, 53 patients received 7mg/kg. Of these, 84.9% achieved ≥16mg/L, and 58.5% reached ≥20mg/L. These results confirm that standard dosing underperforms in the ED setting. For most patients, a 7mg/kg initial dose is necessary to reliably reach concentrations that support effective gentamicin therapy.

Paul Berlin walks. Not in purpose, not with direction, but in the rhythm of the long haul—miles worn into the soles of his boots, days dissolving into the same heat-hazed stretches of jungle and road. He remembers the texture of wet clay clinging to his boot, the way a gear shift rattled in a broken truck, the silence after an explosion that wasn’t loud enough to break. These details press in, not as memory, but as weight. He holds them like proof, as if collecting fragments might somehow form a whole.

The war doesn’t move like a story. It doesn’t unfold in chapters with turning points. Instead, it loops—through tunnels, through ambushes, through long stretches where the horizon stays the same and the enemy might be anywhere or nowhere at all. Cacciato is the one who walks away. Not because he’s fleeing punishment, not because he’s a traitor, but because he walks without stopping, without looking back, as if he’s already somewhere else. That’s how the story begins: not with a decision, but with absence. He’s not a man of ideas or resistance. He doesn’t argue with the war. He doesn’t even seem to notice it. He walks, and that’s enough.

The soldiers chase him, not for justice, not for truth, but because they need to believe in pursuit. The chase is not about catching him. It’s about keeping movement real, keeping the illusion of forward motion alive. The tunnel in "Tunneling Toward Paris" isn’t a metaphor. It’s what happens when the path ends: they fall through, not because they plan to, but because there’s no other way out. The image comes from a book someone once read—Alice, falling—except here, there’s no ladder, no rescue. Just the dark, and then the sky.

Cacciato never thinks. He doesn’t question why they’re there, or whether the war makes sense. He doesn’t carry guilt. He doesn’t even seem to have a name, not really. He’s just the man who walks, and that’s how he stays free. The others are trapped by the need to understand, to explain, to justify. They’re not soldiers. They’re witnesses, cataloging. Paul Berlin counts every detail, but the truth slips through, not because it’s hidden, but because it never settles.

In the end, Sarkin Aung Wan speaks of freedom as a choice, a legacy of old men who wrote about solitude and self-trust. Paul Berlin says nothing. He’s not sure that choice exists anymore. The world doesn’t let you walk away. It makes you stay. But Cacciato did. He walked, and he didn’t look back.

Tibial stress fractures are increasingly tied to overuse injuries driven by repeated microdamage under sustained mechanical strain. During running, ground reaction forces (GRFs) measured by wearable sensors are frequently used as indirect indicators of bone loading. Yet the connection between standard GRF metrics—like impact peak, loading rate, and impulse—and actual tibial compression forces during running remains unclear. This study analyzed vertical GRF parameters in ten healthy individuals across varying running speeds and inclines, comparing them directly to peak tibial load.

The results revealed minimal correspondence between GRF metrics and tibial loading. Correlation coefficients were mostly near zero or weakly negative, with impact peak and loading rate showing r = –0.29 to –0.20. Individual responses varied widely, and only a small subset of participants displayed any meaningful relationship. Of 80 total comparisons, 76 indicated that changes in GRF did not reliably predict shifts in tibial load.

These findings challenge the common assumption that elevated GRFs signal increased bone stress. Since standard GRF measures fail to consistently reflect internal tibial loading, their use in injury risk assessment—especially through wearable devices—may lead to inaccurate conclusions. The mismatch suggests caution in applying GRF data to monitor overuse injury risk in runners.
